title: Rigorous Model Evaluation and Validation
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Rigorous Model Evaluation and Validation ##### The 0.91 that was really 0.63 A demand forecasting team in Mumbai reported 0.91 R² on a five-fold cross-validated model. The number survived three review meetings. Then someone asked how the folds were constructed. `KFold(shuffle=True)`. The data was daily sales per store. Shuffling meant a model trained on 3 March and 5 March was validated on 4 March — predicting a Tuesday when it had already seen Monday and Wednesday for the same store. Sales are strongly autocorrelated; interpolating between two adjacent days is trivial. Forward-chaining validation, training only on the past, gave 0.63. That was the honest number. And it changed the project: 0.63 was not good enough to automate ordering, so the model shipped as a decision-support tool with human review rather than an automated system that would have made confidently wrong orders. Evaluation is not a formality performed after modelling. **It is the thing that determines whether your number means anything**, and the difference between the two protocols here was 0.28 R² and a fundamentally different product decision. ##### Nested cross-validation The subtle problem: when you tune hyperparameters using cross-validation and then report that same cross-validated score, the score is optimistically biased. You selected the configuration that happened to perform best on those particular folds. Cawley and Talbot documented this as **selection bias in model selection**, and showed the inflation can exceed several points on small datasets — enough to reverse a conclusion about which model is better. Nested CV separates the two jobs. The **inner loop** selects hyperparameters; the **outer loop** estimates performance of the entire selection procedure. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Full dataset] --> B[Outer fold 1: hold out 20%] A --> C[Outer fold 2: hold out 20%] A --> D[Outer folds 3-5] B --> E[Inner CV on the 80%:
tune hyperparameters] E --> F[Refit best config on the 80%] F --> G[Score on the held-out 20%] C --> H[Inner CV: tune independently] H --> I[Score on ITS held-out 20%] G --> J[Average the outer scores
= unbiased estimate] I --> J ``` ```python import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.model_selection import (GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV, cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold) from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler import lightgbm as lgb from scipy.stats import randint, loguniform inner_cv = StratifiedKFold(4, shuffle=True, random_state=1) outer_cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) pipe = Pipeline([ ("scale", StandardScaler()), ("clf", lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=42, verbose=-1)), ]) param_dist = { "clf__num_leaves": randint(15, 127), "clf__learning_rate": loguniform(0.01, 0.2), "clf__min_child_samples": randint(5, 100), } search = RandomizedSearchCV(pipe, param_dist, n_iter=25, cv=inner_cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=-1, random_state=42) # The outer loop refits the ENTIRE search on each training split nested = cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=outer_cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=1) # The biased alternative, for comparison search.fit(X, y) biased = search.best_score_ print(f"nested (honest): {nested.mean():.4f} ± {nested.std():.4f}") print(f"non-nested: {biased:.4f}") print(f"optimism: {biased - nested.mean():.4f}") ``` **The cost is real:** nested CV with 5 outer folds and 25 inner trials trains 5 × 25 × 4 = 500 models. Budget accordingly. When to use it: **reporting a final performance estimate**, comparing model families where the comparison must be fair, and any small dataset where the optimism is large. When not to: during exploratory work, and when you have enough data for a genuinely untouched test set — which is simpler and equally honest. A note on what nested CV estimates: it gives you the expected performance of **the whole procedure** (tune, then fit), not of one specific model. The hyperparameters differ across outer folds, and that variation is part of what you are measuring. ##### Time-series and grouped validation The Mumbai failure. Random splitting assumes rows are exchangeable, and they frequently are not. **Time-series** data needs forward chaining — always train on the past, validate on the future: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, test_size=30, gap=7) for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(tscv.split(X)): print(f"fold {i}: train [{tr.min():5d}:{tr.max():5d}] " f"test [{te.min():5d}:{te.max():5d}] " f"train_n={len(tr):5d} test_n={len(te)}") ``` ``` fold 0: train [ 0: 1094] test [ 1102: 1131] train_n= 1095 test_n=30 fold 1: train [ 0: 1124] test [ 1132: 1161] train_n= 1125 test_n=30 fold 2: train [ 0: 1154] test [ 1162: 1191] train_n= 1155 test_n=30 ``` Two arguments matter. **`test_size`** fixes the validation window so folds are comparable. **`gap`** inserts a buffer between train and test — essential when your features use a lookback window, because otherwise the last week of training overlaps with the features of the first validation rows. The **expanding versus rolling** choice is a modelling decision: ```python # Expanding window (TimeSeriesSplit default): train set grows each fold # Rolling window: fixed-length training, discards old data def rolling_origin_split(n, train_size, test_size, step): start = 0 while start + train_size + test_size <= n: yield (np.arange(start, start + train_size), np.arange(start + train_size, start + train_size + test_size)) start += step ``` Use expanding when older data remains relevant; use rolling when the process drifts and old patterns actively mislead. **Grouped data** — multiple rows per entity — needs group-aware splitting: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit # Ensures the same customer never appears in both train and validation gkf = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) for tr, te in gkf.split(X, y, groups=df["customer_id"]): assert not (set(df.customer_id.iloc[tr]) & set(df.customer_id.iloc[te])) ``` And when you have **both** — panel data with repeated observations over time — you need both constraints: ```python def grouped_time_split(df, group_col, time_col, n_splits=5, test_days=30, gap_days=7): """Split by time; groups cannot span the boundary because time is the split key.""" dates = np.sort(df[time_col].unique()) for i in range(n_splits): test_end = dates[-1] - pd.Timedelta(days=test_days * (n_splits - 1 - i)) test_start = test_end - pd.Timedelta(days=test_days) train_end = test_start - pd.Timedelta(days=gap_days) yield (df.index[df[time_col] <= train_end].to_numpy(), df.index[df[time_col].between(test_start, test_end)].to_numpy()) ``` The decision rule, stated plainly: | Data structure | Splitter | |---|---| | Independent rows, balanced target | `KFold(shuffle=True)` | | Independent rows, imbalanced | `StratifiedKFold` | | Repeated entities | `StratifiedGroupKFold` | | Time dimension | `TimeSeriesSplit(gap=...)` | | Both time and groups | Custom, split by time | | Spatial | Spatial blocking | ##### Leakage detection Leakage is information reaching the model that would not be available at prediction time. It is the most common cause of a model that looks excellent and fails in production. The taxonomy, ranked by how often it appears: | Type | Example | Detection | |---|---|---| | **Preprocessing leakage** | Scaler fitted before the split | Pipeline audit | | **Target leakage** | A feature recorded after the outcome | Domain review, feature timing audit | | **Temporal leakage** | Random split on time-series data | Compare random CV to temporal CV | | **Group leakage** | Same customer in train and test | Group overlap check | | **Duplicate leakage** | Near-identical rows across the split | Deduplication before splitting | | **Selection leakage** | Feature selection outside CV | Pipeline audit | A detection harness worth building once and reusing: ```python from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score def leakage_audit(X, y, df=None, group_col=None, time_col=None): findings = [] # 1. Single-feature predictive power — anything above 0.9 is a suspect for c in X.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns: s = X[c].fillna(X[c].median()) try: auc = max(roc_auc_score(y, s), 1 - roc_auc_score(y, s)) if auc > 0.90: findings.append(f"SUSPECT: '{c}' alone achieves AUC {auc:.3f}") except ValueError: continue # 2. Duplicate rows dupes = X.duplicated().sum() if dupes: findings.append(f"{dupes} exact duplicate rows — split them together or drop") # 3. Group overlap across a proposed split if df is not None and group_col: n_groups = df[group_col].nunique() if n_groups < len(df) * 0.9: findings.append(f"Grouped data: {n_groups} groups for {len(df)} rows " f"— use GroupKFold") # 4. Time dimension present but unused if df is not None and time_col: findings.append(f"Time column '{time_col}' present — verify temporal splitting") return findings or ["no obvious leakage detected"] for f in leakage_audit(X, y, df, group_col="customer_id", time_col="order_date"): print(f) ``` The two most powerful diagnostics are comparative rather than absolute. **Random CV versus temporal CV.** A large gap is the signature of temporal leakage: ```python random_score = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42), scoring="average_precision").mean() temporal_score = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5, gap=7), scoring="average_precision").mean() print(f"random CV: {random_score:.4f}") print(f"temporal CV: {temporal_score:.4f}") print(f"gap: {random_score - temporal_score:.4f} (>0.05 investigate)") ``` **The shuffled-label null test.** A pipeline that extracts signal from noise has a leak: ```python def null_test(pipeline, X, y, cv, n_repeats=5, seed=42): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) real = cross_val_score(pipeline, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc").mean() nulls = [cross_val_score(pipeline, X, pd.Series(rng.permutation(y.values)), cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc").mean() for _ in range(n_repeats)] print(f"real: {real:.4f} shuffled: {np.mean(nulls):.4f} ± {np.std(nulls):.4f}") if np.mean(nulls) > 0.55: print("⚠ pipeline finds signal in noise — leakage or overfitting in the CV setup") return real, nulls ``` And the question that catches target leakage, which no code can answer: **for every feature, is this value available at the moment of prediction?** Fields like `resolution_date`, `officer_remark`, `closed_by` and `final_amount` are populated after the outcome and are invisible to every statistical check. ##### Confidence intervals on metrics A single CV score is a point estimate with real uncertainty. Reporting it alone implies precision you do not have. ```python from scipy import stats from sklearn.utils import resample def bootstrap_metric_ci(y_true, y_pred, metric_fn, n_boot=5_000, alpha=0.05, seed=42): """CI from resampling the TEST set — captures test-set sampling variability.""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) n = len(y_true) scores = [] for _ in range(n_boot): idx = rng.integers(0, n, n) if len(np.unique(y_true[idx])) < 2: continue scores.append(metric_fn(y_true[idx], y_pred[idx])) scores = np.array(scores) return (metric_fn(y_true, y_pred), np.percentile(scores, 100 * alpha / 2), np.percentile(scores, 100 * (1 - alpha / 2))) point, lo, hi = bootstrap_metric_ci(y_test.values, probs, average_precision_score) print(f"PR-AUC {point:.4f} 95% CI [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}]") def cv_score_ci(scores, alpha=0.05): """CI from CV fold variability — a DIFFERENT source of uncertainty.""" n = len(scores) se = scores.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n) t = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, df=n - 1) return scores.mean(), scores.mean() - t * se, scores.mean() + t * se ``` **These measure different things**, and conflating them is common. The bootstrap CI captures uncertainty from the finite test set. The CV fold CI captures uncertainty from which rows landed in which fold. Both matter; the bootstrap is usually the one to report for a final held-out evaluation. For a full picture, combine both sources: ```python from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedStratifiedKFold rskf = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=10, random_state=42) scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=rskf, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=-1) mean, lo, hi = cv_score_ci(scores) print(f"{mean:.4f} 95% CI [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}] across {len(scores)} fits") ``` Repeated CV averages over the fold-assignment randomness, giving a more stable estimate at the cost of more compute. ##### Statistically comparing models "Model A scored 0.812 and model B scored 0.807, so A is better" is a claim that needs testing. The critical requirement: **compare on the same folds**, which makes the comparison paired and far more powerful. ```python from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=6, random_state=42) scores_a = cross_val_score(model_a, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=-1) scores_b = cross_val_score(model_b, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision", n_jobs=-1) diffs = scores_a - scores_b print(f"A: {scores_a.mean():.4f} ± {scores_a.std():.4f}") print(f"B: {scores_b.mean():.4f} ± {scores_b.std():.4f}") print(f"mean difference: {diffs.mean():.4f}") # Paired t-test — but the folds are NOT independent, so p is optimistic t_stat, p = stats.ttest_rel(scores_a, scores_b) print(f"paired t-test p = {p:.4f} (treat as optimistic)") # Corrected repeated CV t-test (Nadeau & Bengio) — accounts for fold overlap def corrected_paired_ttest(diffs, n_train, n_test): n = len(diffs) corrected_var = diffs.var(ddof=1) * (1 / n + n_test / n_train) t = diffs.mean() / np.sqrt(corrected_var) return t, 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t), df=n - 1)) t_c, p_c = corrected_paired_ttest(diffs, len(X) * 0.8, len(X) * 0.2) print(f"corrected t-test p = {p_c:.4f}") # Bayesian alternative: probability that A is better by a practically meaningful margin ROPE = 0.005 # differences below this do not matter prob_a_better = (diffs > ROPE).mean() prob_equivalent = (np.abs(diffs) <= ROPE).mean() print(f"P(A better by >{ROPE}) = {prob_a_better:.3f}") print(f"P(practically equivalent) = {prob_equivalent:.3f}") ``` The **corrected t-test** matters because CV folds share training data and are therefore not independent, which makes the standard paired test anti-conservative. Nadeau and Bengio's correction inflates the variance estimate to account for the overlap. The **ROPE** (region of practical equivalence) framing is often more useful than any p-value. A 0.003 AUC difference may be statistically detectable across 30 folds and completely irrelevant to the business. Defining what counts as a meaningful difference **before** running the comparison prevents post-hoc rationalisation. For comparing predictions directly rather than scores, McNemar's test works on the disagreements: ```python from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar pred_a = cross_val_predict(model_a, X, y, cv=cv_single) pred_b = cross_val_predict(model_b, X, y, cv=cv_single) table = [[((pred_a == y) & (pred_b == y)).sum(), ((pred_a == y) & (pred_b != y)).sum()], [((pred_a != y) & (pred_b == y)).sum(), ((pred_a != y) & (pred_b != y)).sum()]] print(mcnemar(table, exact=False, correction=True)) ``` McNemar only uses the cases where the models disagree, which is exactly the relevant information. ##### A validation harness Putting it together into something reusable: ```python from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Callable, Literal @dataclass class ValidationConfig: strategy: Literal["stratified", "grouped", "temporal", "grouped_temporal"] n_splits: int = 5 n_repeats: int = 1 gap: int = 0 group_col: str | None = None time_col: str | None = None scoring: list[str] = field(default_factory=lambda: ["average_precision", "roc_auc"]) def build_cv(cfg: ValidationConfig, df: pd.DataFrame): if cfg.strategy == "stratified": return RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=cfg.n_splits, n_repeats=cfg.n_repeats, random_state=42) if cfg.strategy == "grouped": return StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=cfg.n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=42) if cfg.strategy == "temporal": return TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=cfg.n_splits, gap=cfg.gap) raise ValueError(cfg.strategy) def validate(model, X, y, df, cfg: ValidationConfig) -> pd.DataFrame: cv = build_cv(cfg, df) groups = df[cfg.group_col] if cfg.group_col else None from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate res = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, groups=groups, scoring=cfg.scoring, return_train_score=True, n_jobs=-1) rows = [] for metric in cfg.scoring: test = res[f"test_{metric}"] train = res[f"train_{metric}"] m, lo, hi = cv_score_ci(test) rows.append({"metric": metric, "test_mean": m, "ci_low": lo, "ci_high": hi, "test_std": test.std(), "train_mean": train.mean(), "overfit_gap": train.mean() - test.mean()}) return pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4) ``` The `overfit_gap` column is worth including by default. A large train-test gap is the single most useful diagnostic a validation report can carry, and it costs nothing to compute. ##### Common mistakes - Random splitting on time-series or grouped data. - Reporting a tuned CV score without nesting or a held-out test set. - No gap in `TimeSeriesSplit` when features use a lookback window. - Preprocessing or feature selection outside the pipeline. - A single train/test split on a small dataset, mistaking split luck for performance. - Reporting a point estimate with no confidence interval. - Comparing two models on different folds. - Uncorrected paired t-tests across overlapping CV folds. - No ROPE, so a 0.003 difference gets declared a win. - Never asking whether each feature is available at prediction time. ##### Hands-on Implement nested cross-validation for a tuned model and compare the nested estimate against the non-nested `best_score_` — the optimism gap is the point of the exercise. Then build a correct forward-chaining split for a temporal dataset and contrast the honest score with a naive random-split score, reproducing the Mumbai gap on your own data. Run the leakage audit and the shuffled-label null test on both configurations. For the mini-project, build a validation harness supporting nested CV, grouped CV and time-series CV through one configuration interface. It should report metrics with bootstrap confidence intervals and CV fold intervals separately, include the train-test overfit gap, run the leakage audit automatically, and statistically compare two candidate models using the corrected paired test plus a ROPE analysis. Test it on three datasets with different structures — independent, grouped, temporal — and confirm it selects the right splitter for each. Include a section on what your harness would *not* catch, because knowing the limits is part of using it responsibly. For the assignment, give a concrete example of data leakage in a time-series problem and explain how a proper split prevents it. Include the two numbers — naive and honest — and describe what decision would have been made wrongly on the inflated figure. The Mumbai case is the template; use your own data. ##### Key takeaways - Tuning and reporting on the same folds inflates the score; nested CV or an untouched test set is the fix. - Match the splitter to the data structure — temporal, grouped, or both — and add a gap when features use a lookback. - The gap between random CV and temporal CV is the clearest leakage signature available. - Report confidence intervals, and distinguish test-set uncertainty from fold-assignment uncertainty. - Compare models on the same folds with a corrected paired test, and define practical equivalence before you look.
